rows.themeProjectDescription:
With the rapid development of integrated energy systems, accurate load forecasting is the key to optimizing energy scheduling, improving energy utilization efficiency and ensuring system stable operation. Traditional load forecasting methods have poor adaptability to the nonlinear and fluctuating characteristics of multi‑energy loads. Artificial intelligence algorithms have strong nonlinear fitting ability, which can effectively mine the correlation of load data and improve the accuracy of load forecasting, so it is suitable for the load forecasting research of integrated energy systems.


The main tasks are as follows:


1. Collect and preprocess the historical load data of integrated energy system, including data cleaning, normalization and feature selection;


2. Analyze the influencing factors of heating, power and hydrogen load in integrated energy system;


3. Design and build an artificial intelligence‑based load forecasting model for integrated energy system;


4. Train, optimize and test the forecasting model to improve the forecasting accuracy and generalization ability;


5. Compare and analyze the performance of the proposed model with traditional forecasting methods to verify its effectiveness.


Expected results are as follows:


1. An effective artificial intelligence load forecasting model suitable for integrated energy system;


2. A graduation thesis that systematically summarizes the research process, methods and research conclusions of load forecasting of integrated energy system based on artificial intelligence.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Background:


Under the trend of device miniaturization in advanced packaging, advanced packaging has been regarded as one of the important technologies to break through Moore's Law. However, the warpage deformation caused by the mismatch of thermal expansion coefficients (CTE) between packaging materials is a major obstacle to the development of advanced packaging, and at the same time, the service environment of solder joints becomes more severe, which puts forward higher reliability requirements for solder joint materials. Therefore, the research on warpage and solder joint reliability is very important.


Main task:

Aiming at the thermally induced warpage in 2.5D/3D packaging, provide its theoretical modeling combined with simulation verification, and based on appropriate optimization methods, provide corresponding optimized design schemes. Aiming at the reliability research of BGA solder joints in 2.5D/3D packaging, through COMSOL simulation, conduct reliability analysis on various indicators of the solder joints (plastic deformation, viscoplastic dissipation energy density, life, etc.).


Expected outcomes:

1. Establish a complete theoretical model that can predict thermally induced warpage in various advanced packaging, and verify the accuracy of the model by combining COMSOL simulation;

2. Select one packaging form in 2.5D/3D packaging to conduct a complete analysis on the reliability research of its BGA solder joints.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Speech keyword recognition is an important task in human-computer interaction, smart devices, voice control systems, and edge intelligence applications. Compared with full automatic speech recognition, keyword recognition focuses on detecting a limited set of predefined commands, such as “yes”, “no”, “stop”, or “go”, which makes it suitable for low-power and real-time systems. With the development of deep learning, neural-network-based methods have achieved significantly better recognition performance than traditional hand-crafted feature and template-matching approaches. However, many deep learning models still suffer from high computational cost and large parameter size, which may limit their deployment on resource-constrained devices. Therefore, this project aims to study and implement a deep learning-based speech keyword recognition method with a balance between recognition accuracy and model efficiency.


2. Main Task

The main task of this project is to design, train, and evaluate a speech keyword recognition model based on deep learning. The student is expected to complete audio data preprocessing, including waveform loading, resampling, normalization, and feature extraction using Mel-spectrogram or MFCC features. A baseline neural network, such as CNN, CRNN, or a lightweight deep learning model, will be implemented using Python and PyTorch or TensorFlow. The model will be trained and tested on a public speech keyword dataset, such as Google Speech Commands. The project should compare at least two model structures or settings, and analyze their performance in terms of recognition accuracy, parameter size, computational complexity, and inference time.


3. Expected Outcomes

The expected outcome is a complete deep learning-based speech keyword recognition system. The target is to achieve a recognition accuracy of over 90% on a standard test set for selected keywords. The student is also expected to complete a well-structured FYP report, source code, trained model files, and a simple demonstration program that can recognize speech commands from audio samples.

Known-class feature representations are obtained through neural networks; subsequently, two orthogonal subspaces of the known-class feature matrix are derived. Using the ratio of feature projections within these two subspaces as a metric, a decision is made on whether a radiation source signal sample belongs to a known class. The graduation project requires completing the study of this algorithm, implementing simulations on open datasets, and finishing the graduation thesis.

1. Background

The lamp posts on campus are mostly square-shaped and made of iron. Currently, they are cleaned manually using a soft long-pole duster. This method only lightly sweeps the underside of the lamp shades, offering limited cleaning effect, and leaves the post body untouched. As a result, dust and dirt accumulate on both the posts and the shades. This project aims to design a robot that can climb the post, clean its surfaces, and thoroughly wipe the undersides of the lamp shades using magnetic adhesion and vision guided control.

2. Main Task

Design and build a prototype robot that:

  • Attaches to a square iron post via a hinge and latch frame.
  • Climbs using electro permanent magnets and a lead screw stepper motor (peristaltic motion).
  • Cleans the post surfaces with roller brushes.
  • Uses USB camera(s) with Python/OpenCV to detect lamp shades.
  • Deploys two L shaped cleaning arms to wipe the underside of each lamp shade.
  • Is controlled by a laptop (vision & state machine) and a microcontroller (e.g., STM32, Arduino, or Raspberry Pi) for low level motor, servo, and magnet drivers.

The prototype will be tested on a 1.5 m mock up post.

3. Expected Outcomes

  • A functional prototype robot capable of climbing the post, detecting lamp shades, and cleaning the post and lamps.
  • Design documentation (description of the mechanical structure, circuit schematics, system block diagram).
  • Source code (microcontroller firmware, Python vision and control scripts).
  • A short demonstration video (2–3 minutes).

1. Background

Circuit drawing homework is a core assessment task in electronic engineering courses. At present, teachers rely entirely on manual checking to judge component errors, connection faults and circuit logic mistakes, which brings heavy repetitive workload. Manual grading also suffers from inconsistent scoring standards and delayed feedback for students. Existing graphic recognition tools only support simple circuit digitization, lacking targeted topological matching and automatic scoring functions oriented to teaching evaluation. This FYP designs an end-to-end automatic grading system for circuit diagrams based on digital image processing and lightweight target detection algorithms. The system targets both software-drawn standard circuit diagrams and hand-drawn student sketches, and realizes intelligent identification, error detection and quantitative scoring.

  1. 2. Main TaskBuild a self-made circuit diagram dataset containing 300+ images, covering common electronic components (resistor, triode, logic gate, etc.), including 150 hand-drawn samples and 150 standard digital drawings; complete image labeling for component bounding boxes and wire topological nodes.
  2. Train a lightweight YOLOv8 model for circuit component recognition, with a target mAP@0.5 no less than 90%; adopt morphological algorithms and Hough transform to extract circuit wires, and establish an adjacency list to store circuit topological relations.
  3. Design a graph matching algorithm to compare student circuit topology with standard reference circuits, automatically identify 6 common error types: missing components, wrong component types, open circuits, short circuits, incorrect pin connections and wrong component parameters.
  4. Formulate quantitative scoring rules with adjustable weight coefficients for different error types, and develop a PyQt graphical interface supporting image import, error marking, automatic score output and class error statistics charts.
  5. Complete system performance testing: the overall automatic grading accuracy should reach over 90% compared with manual teacher scoring, and the single-image processing speed is controlled within 5 seconds on ordinary desktop CPUs.

3. Expected Outcomes

  1. A complete labeled circuit diagram dataset with 300+ images and corresponding annotation files.
  2. Lightweight circuit component detection model and full set of Python algorithm source code for wire extraction, topological matching and error judgment.
  3. A runnable desktop automatic grading GUI software with editable scoring rule configuration module.
  4. A systematic test report recording recognition precision, grading accuracy and running speed of the system under different circuit types.
  5. Complete graduation thesis and project demonstration video showing the whole workflow from uploading circuit images to generating grading feedback.

Division of Labor (for group project)

  1. Member A (Algorithm Module Responsible): Dataset collection & labeling, YOLOv8 model training and optimization, image preprocessing and wire extraction algorithm development, performance indicator testing.
  2. Member B (System & Application Responsible): Circuit topological matching logic coding, automatic scoring rule design, PyQt human-computer interface development, data statistics and chart visualization function realization.
  3. Member C (Documentation & Verification Responsible): Test case design for hand-drawn and standard circuits, comparison between system grading results and manual teacher scores, sorting test reports, compiling the full graduation thesis and demonstration materials.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background: With the scaling of advanced semiconductor process nodes, electrostatic discharge (ESD) protection for integrated circuit ports faces severe challenges. In some application scenarios, due to the possibility of pin voltages being lower than ground potential, there is an urgent need for bipolar devices that can provide effective clamping protection in both positive and negative directions. Traditional bidirectional SCR structures often suffer from the problem of excessively low holding voltage. In recent years, the holding voltage of devices has been effectively improved by introducing self-biased gates and additional implantation regions. The latest research further shows that the adoption of a three-implantation region design including an N-drift region can significantly improve current distribution and reduce dynamic resistance in high-voltage applications. However, how to balance various electrical indicators and the thermal stability degradation mechanism of the device in the extreme high-temperature environment from 300K to 500K remain the key core difficulties in current protection design. This project aims to reveal the complex multi-physics coupling mechanism inside the new bidirectional SCR through numerical simulation.


2. Main task: 1. Literature analysis and physical mechanism combing: Systematically study core literature to clarify the underlying structural evolution logic and feedback physical essence of bidirectional SCR devices from "introducing P+ regions to reduce trigger voltage", "self-biased gates to improve holding voltage" to "N-drift three-implantation regions to reduce dynamic resistance". 2. Two-dimensional TCAD device modeling and benchmark transient simulation: Use the Sentaurus TCAD simulation platform to construct a two-dimensional cross-sectional model of the bidirectional SCR including P+ bridge regions, self-biased gates, and N-drift regions. Reasonably configure carrier mobility, avalanche breakdown, and recombination models. Under TLP pulse (10ns rising edge) transient excitation, obtain transient and quasi-static characteristic curves and key physical parameters such as internal electric field and carrier concentration. 3. Joint regulation of key structural parameters and law induction (core task): Design multi-variable orthogonal scanning experiments for the core design variables in the literature. Systematically explore the joint constraints of different structural size combinations on trigger voltage, holding voltage, and secondary breakdown current, and optimize the design window as much as possible. 4. Thermal stability and internal field evolution analysis under extreme working conditions (core task): Introduce the ambient temperature gradient from 300K to 500K as the core variable. Carry out thermodynamics and electrical simulations, deeply extract and compare the collision ionization rate, carrier recombination rate, and electrostatic potential distribution inside the device at different temperatures. Analyze the influence of high temperature on key parameters such as trigger voltage and holding voltage.


3. Expected outcomes: 1. Establishment of simulation engineering library: Submit a set of structurally complete and code-standard new bidirectional SCR device Sentaurus TCAD simulation engineering file libraries, covering the complete process from device construction to TLP transient simulation. 2. Multidimensional feature data visualization analysis: Proficiency in using SVisual post-processing tools to accurately read simulation output data files. Draw comparative I-V characteristic curves under multiple sets of key variables, as well as two-dimensional color contour maps of internal electric field and carrier concentration, and be able to analyze and explain from the underlying physical mechanism. 3. Construct an electro-thermal coupling simulation model for a wide temperature range (300K-500K), accurately quantify the thermal degradation law of bidirectional SCR trigger characteristics and holding voltage; and accurately define the thermal failure boundary of the device, providing rigorous theoretical support and optimization criteria for the anti-thermal degradation design of high-reliability ESD protection structures. 4. Standardized academic report and presentation: Write a logically rigorous and format-standardized final report, deeply explaining parameter optimization laws and high-temperature degradation mechanisms. And make an academic report based on core research conclusions.
rows.themeTitle: Simulation Study on ESD Protection Mechanism and Thermal Stability of High-Voltage Bidirectional SCR Device with N-drift and Self-biased Gate Structure

1. Background

The BeiDou Navigation Satellite System has become a major enabling technology for positioning, navigation, timing, and intelligent applications in China and beyond. In recent years, low-altitude economy, intelligent transportation, unmanned systems, and infrastructure inspection have all created increasing demand for high-accuracy and high-reliability positioning solutions. In Hainan, this demand is particularly relevant due to the development of coastal transportation, island logistics, low-altitude UAV applications, and digital infrastructure management.

However, standalone BeiDou positioning performance may degrade in practical scenarios due to signal blockage, multipath, limited satellite visibility, atmospheric disturbances, and temporary interruptions. For intelligent inspection tasks using drones or mobile platforms, positioning continuity is as important as positioning accuracy. Integrating BeiDou with an inertial navigation system (INS) is a practical and widely adopted solution, where inertial sensing provides short-term continuity and GNSS provides long-term correction.

2. Main Task

This project aims to develop a BeiDou/INS integrated positioning method for low-altitude intelligent inspection applications. The student will first study the principles of BeiDou positioning, inertial sensor errors, coordinate systems, motion modeling, and data fusion algorithms. The project may use public GNSS/IMU datasets, simulation data, or small-scale experimental datadepending on resource availability.

The main technical work is to implement and evaluate a fusion algorithm based on Kalman Filter, Extended Kalman Filter, Unscented Kalman Filter, or equivalent sensor fusion schemes. The system should estimate position, velocity, and possibly attitude information, and compare the performance of standalone BeiDou, standalone INS dead reckoning, and integrated BeiDou/INS solutions. The student is encouraged to consider realistic scenarios such as partial signal blockage or short GNSS outages of 5–20 seconds.

Quantitative objectives may include reducing positioning error by at least 30% compared with standalone BeiDou under degraded signal conditions, maintaining continuous trajectory output during simulated outages, and achieving stable trajectory reconstruction in representative inspection scenarios.

3. Expected Outcomes

Expected outcomes include a BeiDou/INS positioning algorithm, a simulation or experimental evaluation platform, and a quantitative comparison of different positioning strategies. The final system should demonstrate improved accuracy, continuity, and robustness in low-altitude or mobile inspection scenarios. The dissertation should include theoretical modeling, algorithm implementation, trajectory analysis, and error statistics under multiple test conditions. This project is especially suitable for students interested in navigation, intelligent systems, low-altitude applications, and BeiDou-enabled engineering innovation.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Communication and navigation systems increasingly operate in dense and complex electromagnetic environments, where different forms of intentional or unintentional interference may significantly degrade system reliability and service quality. In wireless communication systems, interference may reduce throughput and increase bit error rate; in navigation systems, especially satellite-based systems such as BeiDou, interference may cause signal loss, tracking failure, or severe positioning degradation. Therefore, accurate recognition of interference types is an important prerequisite for adaptive anti-jamming and interference mitigation.

Traditional interference recognition methods typically rely on manually designed features derived from the spectrum, energy distribution, bandwidth, or statistical properties of the received signal. These methods are often limited when dealing with low signal-to-noise ratio, mixed interference, or highly dynamic signal environments. By combining time-frequency analysis with deep learning, interference recognition can be formulated as a data-driven pattern classification problem, allowing automatic extraction of discriminative features from spectrogram-like representations.

2. Main Task

This project aims to investigate intelligent recognition of communication/navigation interference signals using time-frequency analysis and deep learning techniques. The student will first model or simulate several representative interference types, such as single-tone interference, multi-tone interference, narrowband interference, broadband noise interference, chirp interference, pulsed interference, and sweep interference. A dataset containing around 5,000–15,000 signal samples under different SNR or JSR conditions is recommended.

The student will then generate time-frequency representations using methods such as Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), wavelet transform, or other suitable approaches, and compare their effectiveness. Based on these representations, a classifier using CNN, ResNet, MobileNet, Vision Transformer, or a hybrid deep network will be designed and trained. The project should compare multiple architectures and evaluate robustness under different noise levels, especially under low-SNR conditions.

Quantitative research targets may include classification accuracy of above 90% under moderate conditions and above 80% under low-SNR scenarios, together with clear confusion matrix analysis and robustness evaluation.

3. Expected Outcomes

Expected outcomes include a simulated interference dataset, a complete time-frequency feature extraction and classification pipeline, and a trained deep learning model for interference recognition. The final report should demonstrate the ability of the proposed method to distinguish multiple interference categories with satisfactory robustness. Evaluation should include accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, confusion matrix, and sensitivity to SNR/JSR variations. This topic is well aligned with the strengths of electronic information engineering, intelligent signal processing, and communication systems, and is particularly suitable for students considering postgraduate study in communications, signal processing, or navigation.

1. Background

Roads and bridges are key components of modern transportation infrastructure, and their service safety is closely related to regular inspection and maintenance. Surface defects such as cracks, potholes, spalling, exposed reinforcement, and water seepage may gradually develop into serious structural problems if not identified at an early stage. Conventional manual inspection methods are often labor-intensive, subjective, slow, and difficult to scale, especially in large-area or hard-to-access scenarios. With recent advances in deep learning and computer vision, image-based automatic defect detection has become a highly promising approach for intelligent infrastructure inspection.

For Hainan and similar coastal or rapidly developing regions, the need for efficient transportation maintenance and digital infrastructure management is increasing. Therefore, a practical and lightweight AI-based detection system is of clear engineering relevance. Since deployment on mobile or edge devices is desirable in real applications, both detection accuracy and computational efficiency should be considered.

2. Main Task

This project aims to develop a lightweight deep learning framework for automatic detection and quantitative assessment of road and bridge surface defects. The student will first review common defect categories and prepare a labeled dataset using public data and/or self-collected images. A dataset of approximately 1,500–3,000 images covering at least 4–6 common defect typesis recommended. The project will then implement a baseline model using architectures such as YOLOv8, YOLOv10, RT-DETR, or lightweight segmentation networks, followed by optimization for small-target detection, robustness under illumination variation, and reduced model complexity.

Possible technical improvements include data augmentation, attention mechanisms, lightweight backbones, pruning, and feature fusion strategies. In addition to defect localization, the student is encouraged to explore basic quantitative indicators such as crack length, defect area, or severity level estimation. The target is to achieve mAP@0.5 above 80% , with an inference speed suitable for near real-time testing, e.g., above 15–20 FPS on a standard GPU platform.

3. Expected Outcomes

Expected outcomes include a defect image dataset, a trained lightweight detection model, a comparative evaluation against baseline methods, and a prototype interface for result visualization. The final system should be able to identify major surface defects and provide basic quantitative inspection outputs. The dissertation is expected to include model design, experimental validation, ablation studies, and performance comparison in terms of precision, recall, F1-score, mAP, inference speed, and model size. This project is suitable for students interested in AI, computer vision, and intelligent infrastructure applications.

1. Background


Network traffic measurement plays a fundamental role in modern network

management by providing essential traffic state information for tasks

such as anomaly detection, load balancing, and quality-of-service

assurance. However, due to the severely constrained memory and

computational resources of commodity switches, achieving fine-grained

and accurate traffic measurement at scale remains a significant

challenge. To improve measurement efficiency under resource constraints,

network-level collaborative measurement has emerged as a promising

approach. Rather than measuring all traffic independently at each

switch, measurement tasks are distributed across multiple switch nodes

in a coordinated manner, avoiding redundant monitoring of the same

flow and enabling each switch to focus on a distinct subset of

passing traffic. This collaborative paradigm improves both resource

utilization and measurement accuracy across the network. Nevertheless, the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of real-world

network traffic makes static task allocation strategies inadequate.

The measurement workload varies continuously across switches, and

suboptimal allocation decisions can lead to coverage gaps or resource

waste. This project addresses the dynamic allocation of collaborative

measurement tasks through a multi-agent reinforcement learning

framework, in which distributed switch agents learn to coordinate

their measurement strategies adaptively in response to evolving

traffic conditions, without requiring centralized control or

prior knowledge of traffic distributions.

（1）Study the fundamental principles of data center networks;

（3）Learn typical reinforcement learning methods;




（4）Design a cooperative traffic measurement method based on muti-agent reinforcement learning algorithms;




（5）Perform simulation validation and continuous improvement of the proposed algorithm;




（6）Complete the undergraduate thesis.






3. Expected outcomes




(1) An intelligent system for cooperative network traffic measurement;

rows.themeProjectDescription: The concentration and particle size distribution of suspended particles in solution are important parameters for assessing water quality, pharmaceutical purity, and the quality of chemical liquids. This project aims to develop a rapid detection method based on the principle of light scattering. When a light beam passes through a solution containing particles, scattered light is generated at specific angles. The intensity of the scattered light is proportional to the particle concentration, while the angular distribution of the scattered light is related to the particle size. This research plans to design a miniature optical path system, using a laser light source and high-sensitivity photodetectors, to construct a portable detection device. By measuring the scattered light intensity and angular distribution, combined with inversion calculations based on the Mie scattering model, the project aims to achieve simultaneous quantitative analysis of particle concentration and size. This method requires no complex pretreatment, offers rapid response, and is non-contact and non-destructive. It is expected to provide an efficient, online tool for particle detection in environmental monitoring, the pharmaceutical industry, and process control.

rows.themeProjectDescription: Polymer optical waveguides hold significant application value in the fields of integrated photonics and optical interconnects. This project aims to develop a high-precision, rapid fabrication method for polymer optical waveguides by combining digital light processing (DLP) technology with a light-induced self-writing polymer process. Utilizing the high-resolution dynamic masking capability of DLP technology, a pre-designed patterned light beam is projected into a photosensitive polymer precursor solution. Localized photopolymerization is initiated by the light, enabling one-step self-writing formation of the waveguide structure, thereby avoiding the complex mask fabrication and development steps inherent in traditional photolithography. The study will systematically investigate the effects of exposure dosage, light intensity distribution, and polymer formulation on the waveguide geometry and optical performance, and will characterize key parameters such as propagation loss and mode coupling. This work aims to establish a flexible and efficient new strategy for polymer optical waveguide manufacturing, providing technical support for the development of on-chip optical interconnects, optical sensing, and flexible photonic devices.

Biopotential signals such as ECG, EEG, and EMG are typically weak, low-frequency, and easily affected by electrode-skin impedance, motion artifacts, power-line interference, and circuit noise. The main tasks include literature review, specification definition, circuit architecture design, transistor-level circuit implementation, simulation verification, and performance evaluation. Forest fires are important ecological and environmental disturbances that can cause vegetation loss, biodiversity degradation, soil erosion, carbon emissions, and threats to human life and property. Sichuan Province has complex topography, diverse climate conditions, rich forest resources, and significant spatial differences in vegetation types and human activities. These factors make forest fire occurrence highly heterogeneous in both space and time. In recent years, climate variability, extreme weather events, land use change, and increasing human activities have further influenced forest fire risk. Understanding the spatiotemporal evolution characteristics of forest fires in Sichuan Province is therefore important for fire prevention, ecological protection, disaster risk management, and sustainable forest resource planning. Attribution analysis can help identify the key driving factors behind fire occurrence and provide scientific support for regional forest fire monitoring and early warning.

Main Task:

The main task of this project is to analyze the spatiotemporal distribution patterns and possible driving factors of forest fires in Sichuan Province. The student will first conduct a literature review on forest fire monitoring, spatial-temporal pattern analysis, and fire attribution methods. Then, forest fire occurrence data will be collected and organized, which may include satellite fire point products, burned area datasets, meteorological data, vegetation indices, topographic data, land use data, and human activity indicators. Data preprocessing may include coordinate transformation, spatial matching, temporal aggregation, missing value processing, and construction of analysis units. Based on these datasets, the student will analyze the temporal variation of forest fires at annual, seasonal, and monthly scales, and investigate spatial clustering, hotspot distribution, and regional differences. Furthermore, attribution analysis will be conducted to explore the influence of factors such as temperature, precipitation, wind speed, humidity, elevation, slope, vegetation coverage, land use type, population density, and distance to roads or settlements. Possible methods include correlation analysis, regression models, random forest, geographic detector, or spatial statistical methods.

The expected outcome of this project includes a structured forest fire dataset for Sichuan Province, a set of spatiotemporal analysis results, attribution analysis of major driving factors, source code or GIS workflows, and visualized maps and charts. The project should identify the key natural and human-related factors associated with forest fire occurrence and explain their possible mechanisms. The final results may provide useful reference for forest fire prevention, risk zoning, ecological management, and disaster mitigation. Through this project, the student will gain practical experience in remote sensing data processing, GIS spatial analysis, environmental data integration, statistical modeling, and scientific thesis writing.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1 Background

State Space Models (SSMs), particularly Mamba, have emerged as a compelling alternative to Transformers, offering linear computational complexity in long-sequence modeling while maintaining competitive performance. However, the growing parameter sizes of SSMs create significant deployment challenges on resource-constrained edge devices. Model compression techniques—structured pruning, quantization, and low-rank decomposition—are essential for lightweight deployment, but they introduce complex trade-offs among compression ratio, inference speed, accuracy retention, and hardware energy efficiency. Traditional single-objective compression approaches fail to capture these competing demands. Multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) such as NSGA-II and MOEA/D provide a principled framework for navigating these trade-offs by generating Pareto-optimal solution sets. Furthermore, assessing compression strategies solely on GPU metrics overlooks the energy efficiency characteristics of emerging compute-in-memory (CIM) accelerators, which are critical for embodied AI applications. CIM-MLC (architecture-level) and NeuroSim (circuit-level) are two complementary simulation tools for CIM energy estimation.

2 Main Task

This project develops an automated multi-objective compression framework for SSMs that jointly optimizes four objectives:

(i) model compression ratio,

(ii) inference throughput,

(iii) accuracy retention on downstream tasks, and

(iv) energy efficiency on CIM simulators.

The student will first survey SSM architectures (Mamba, Mamba2) and compression methodologies. Then, a modular compression pipeline will be implemented, supporting structured pruning, INT8/FP16 quantization, and low-rank factorization. NSGA-II and MOEA/D will be integrated to search the high-dimensional configuration space, with Pareto front convergence analysis across algorithms. Critically, compressed models will be evaluated not only on standard benchmarks (e.g., long-range arena) but also on CIM simulators to quantify actual energy-performance trade-offs. The primary evaluation tool is CIM-MLC; NeuroSim can be used as an alternative circuit-level estimator.

Tasks

• Survey SSM architecture fundamentals (Mamba, Mamba2) and existing model compression techniques

• Formulate SSM compression as a multi-objective optimization problem (compression ratio vs. accuracy vs. speed vs. energy)

• Implement a compression evaluation pipeline supporting pruning, quantization, and low-rank decomposition

• Apply NSGA-II and MOEA/D to search optimal compression configurations and compare their Pareto fronts

• Evaluate compressed SSM models on long-sequence benchmarks and CIM simulators (CIM-MLC primary, NeuroSim alternative) for energy-performance trade-offs

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Multi-unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems are required to perform full-coverage scanning over extensive target areas for missions such as border patrol, post-disaster area assessment and large-scale farm monitoring. In practical operations, UAVs are subject to multiple constraints, including limited communication bandwidth caused by signal attenuation and interference, restricted communication range that may lead to disconnection beyond effective coverage, as well as battery capacity limitations characterized by short endurance and mandatory return for recharging. Traditional coverage planning methods generally assume ideal communication conditions and unlimited energy supply, which often results in communication outages or power depletion during actual flight. It remains a challenging task to achieve complete area coverage via cooperative planning of multiple UAVs under dual constraints of communication and energy, while minimizing total energy consumption and flight duration. This project investigates cooperative coverage planning strategies for multi-UAV systems with communication and energy limitations, aiming to enhance the robustness and practicality of the overall system. The main research tasks are specified as follows:

1) Constraint Modeling and Problem Formalization

Establish UAV communication range models, signal attenuation models (e.g., free-space path loss model) and energy consumption models correlated with flight speed, travel distance and payload. Formulate communication connectivity constraints requiring each UAV to maintain connection with at least one in-range UAV, and energy feasibility constraints stipulating that the total energy consumption of flight paths shall not exceed battery capacity. The cooperative coverage planning problem is ultimately formalized as a constrained combinatorial optimization problem.

2) Area Decomposition and Coverage PathGeneration

Propose an area decomposition approach based on grid graphs or Voronoi diagrams to partition the large target region into multiple subregions and assign each subregion to individual UAVs. For each divided subregion, generate global coverage paths adopting Boustrophedon scanning or spiral coverage patterns. The number of turns is further optimized to reduce overall energy consumption.

3) Communication Relay and Energy Coordination Strategy

Develop an inter-UAV communication relay mechanism. When a UAV suffers weak signals due to excessive distance from the base station, another UAV will be dynamically scheduled as a relay node to sustain the connectivity of the entire UAV swarm. Meanwhile, an energy-balanced task scheduling scheme is designed to assign more coverage tasks to UAVs with sufficient remaining power, so as to prevent early return of individual UAVs.

4) Simulation Validation and Performance Evaluation

Construct a large-scale outdoor simulation environment with undulating terrain sized at 500 m × 500 m using Gazebo or AirSim, where 3 to 5 quadrotor UAVs are deployed. Comparative experiments are conducted against classic coverage planning without constraint consideration, schemes with only energy constraints and schemes with only communication constraints. Evaluation metrics include full coverage rate, maximum variance of energy consumption, number of communication interruptions and total mission time. A visualization interface is also developed to display real-time communication link status and residual energy during cooperative coverage operations.
rows.themeTitle: Research on collaborative coverage planning for multi-UAV systems under communication and energy constraints

rows.themeProjectDescription:
After the occurrence of natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods and wildfires, cooperative search and rescue (SAR) with multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can rapidly cover large-scale complex terrains and improve the efficiency of survivor detection. Nevertheless, the SAR environment presents

multiple challenges, including uneven distribution of mission points, limited endurance of UAVs, dynamically changing communication topologies, and time-decaying mission values. These characteristics render traditional task allocation methods incapable of real-time adaptation to dynamic scenarios. Moreover, such methods lack the capability to structurally model the complex interactions among agents, thus failing to achieve real-time and efficient task allocation. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) can effectively represent the heterogeneous relational graph between UAVs and missions, and learn optimal allocation strategies by exploiting topological information. Accordingly, this project leverages the representation learning capability of GNNs for non-Euclidean data to investigate multi-UAV task allocation methods tailored for SAR scenarios, aiming to maximize overall search-and-rescue benefits and minimize mission completion time. The main research contents are outlined as follows:

1) SAR Scenario Modeling and Graph Construction

Formulate the multi-UAV SAR task allocation problem in a formal manner. UAVs and mission points are defined as two types of nodes in a heterogeneous graph. Edge features incorporate the distance from UAVs to mission points, mission priority, time window constraints and communication topological relationships.

A dynamic task allocation model is established based on Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (Dec-POMDP).

2) Design of GNN-based Allocation Strategy

Develop a task allocation decision module based on Graph Attention Networks (GAT) or Graph Isomorphism Networks (GIN). Features of neighboring UAVs and missions are aggregated via message passing to output the allocation probability or marginal benefit of each UAV for individual missions. The Hungarian algorithm or greedy matching is adopted to convert probability outputs into feasible task allocation schemes.

3) Online Reallocation Mechanism for Dynamic Environments

To address dynamic events during SAR operations, including newly detected missions, UAV malfunctions and return-to-base for recharging, an incremental GNN-based task reallocation approach is proposed. By exploiting the locality of graph topology, only the embeddings of affected nodes are updated, so as to realize

low-latency online re-planning.

4) Simulation Verification and Performance Comparison

Construct SAR simulation environments based on AirSim or ROS combined with Gazebo, which cover terrains with obstacles, 10 to 20 mission points and 3 to 5 UAVs. Comparative experiments are conducted against classic greedy allocation, the Hungarian algorithm and reinforcement learning-based allocation methods. The

performance of the proposed method is evaluated in terms of mission completion rate, total flight distance and reallocation response time. Meanwhile, a visualization interface is developed to dynamically display the allocation graph and UAV flight paths during the whole process.
rows.themeTitle: Graph neural network based task allocation method for multi-UAV search and rescue missions

This project focuses on the reliability of through-glass vias (TGVs) used in advanced packaging after thermal cycling. Due to the mismatch in thermal expansion between glass, metal filling materials, and redistribution layers, repeated temperature changes may induce thermal stress, leading to cracks, interfacial delamination, resistance increase, or open-circuit failure.


2. Main Task

The student will review the basic structure, fabrication process, and reliability challenges of TGVs. Thermal cycling tests will be analyzed under temperature ranges. Electrical resistance changes, surface morphology, via defects, cracks, and delamination will be characterized using suitable testing and inspection methods. The relationship between thermal cycling conditions and failure behavior will be analyzed.


3. Expected Outcomes

The project is expected to obtain reliability evaluation results of TGV samples after thermal cycling, including resistance variation, defect observation, and failure mode analysis. The student should summarize the main factors affecting TGV reliability and propose possible improvements in via structure, metallization, material selection, or processing conditions.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
In advanced packaging systems, excessive temperature can reduce device reliability, accelerate material degradation, increase thermal stress, and affect the long-term performance of interconnects. Therefore, effective heat dissipation design for glass-based packaging substrates is becoming an important research topic. One possible solution is to introduce microchannels into glass substrates, allowing coolant or working fluid to flow through the substrate and remove heat directly from the heat-generating area. Glass-based microfluidic cooling structures have the potential to combine electrical insulation, optical transparency, chemical resistance, and embedded thermal management in one platform.


The main tasks of this project are as follows:

Design one or more glass-based microchannel structures, such as straight channels, parallel channels, serpentine channels, or inlet–outlet manifold structures.

Define the key geometrical parameters of the microchannels, including channel width, depth, length, spacing, inlet/outlet diameter, and overall substrate size.

Analyze the effects of flow rate, channel size, channel layout, and heat flux on temperature distribution, maximum temperature, pressure drop, and cooling uniformity.

Discuss the possible fabrication routes for glass-based microchannels, such as wet etching, laser processing, mechanical micromachining, and glass bonding.


By the end of the project, the student is expected to achieve the following outcomes:

A clear understanding of the thermal management challenges of glass substrates in advanced packaging applications.

A complete design of a glass-based microchannel cooling structure, including layout drawings and key dimensional parameters.

A simulation model for analyzing fluid flow and heat transfer in the microchannel structure.

Quantitative results showing the relationship between channel geometry, flow rate, pressure drop, and cooling performance.

A possible final deliverable is a glass-based microchannel cooling design capable of reducing the peak substrate temperature by a measurable amount under a defined heat flux, while keeping the pressure drop within a practical operating range.

1. Background

Emotion recognition is the core research direction in the field of affective computing, which has important application prospects in mental health monitoring and personalized medical services. Traditional emotion recognition methods mainly rely on external manifestations such as facial expressions and voice signals, which are easily interfered by subjective factors such as facial masking and emotional disguise, resulting in limited recognition accuracy and poor robustness. Physiological signals such as EEG (Electroencephalogram), ECG (Electrocardiogram) and GSR (Galvanic Skin Response) can objectively reflect the internal emotional changes of the human body without being affected by subjective disguise, and have become reliable data sources for high-precision emotion recognition. With the rapid development of multi-modal feature fusion and lightweight deep learning technologies, researches on feature alignment, heterogeneous data fusion and emotion classification based on multi-modal physiological signals have gradually become a hot spot. Existing studies have verified that combining EEG, ECG and GSR signals can significantly improve the generalization ability of emotion recognition models. However, there are still problems such as signal heterogeneity, redundant feature information, large model parameters and difficulty in balancing accuracy and inference speed. This topic relies on public datasets AMIGOS and ASCERTAIN, aiming to design a lightweight emotion recognition algorithm integrating cross-modal feature alignment and context perception. By optimizing the preprocessing workflow, feature fusion strategy and network architecture, this method can effectively solve the problems of inconsistent modal distribution and excessive model complexity.

[2].JJoshi, S., & Srinivas, L. N. B. (2025). An ensemble classifier for emotion classification from EEG and GSR signals for autism detection. Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine, 270, 108921.

Networks, 187, 107363.


2. Main Tasks


1. Multimodal physiological signal preprocessing and feature engineering: Preprocess multimodal physiological signals including electroencephalogram (EEG), electrocardiogram (ECG) and galvanic skin response (GSR), and then conduct multi-dimensional feature extraction, so as to provide a solid data foundation for subsequent model analysis.

2. Cross-modal feature alignment and fusion model: Integrate feature alignment algorithms with signal fusion strategies to unify the representation forms of heterogeneous multimodal data. Meanwhile, construct a lightweight network architecture to balance recognition accuracy and model structural compactness.

3. Algorithm optimization and evaluation: Optimize and iterate the model by adopting network pruning and other lightweight methods. Multiple evaluation metrics are adopted to comprehensively assess the overall performance of the model. Finally, a series of comparative experiments are carried out to analyze the inference speed of different models and complete the performance verification of the overall algorithm.


3.Expected Outcomes

(1) A complete set of multi-modal physiological signal preprocessing and feature extraction code library.

(2) A lightweight emotion recognition model with classification accuracy ≥75%.

(3) Algorithm performance optimization analysis report and graduation thesis.

Project Background & Motivation:

IPSec (Internet Protocol Security) is a widely used protocol suite for securing IP communications through authentication and encryption. VPN (Virtual Private Network) implementations based on IPSec are critical for secure data transmission over untrusted networks such as the Internet. However, software-based IPSec processing on embedded ARM systems suffers from high computational overhead due to cryptographic operations (e.g., AES, SHA) and packet processing, leading to low throughput and high latency. This project aims to design a high-performance IPSec VPN module by combining an ARM processor with custom IP acceleration cores for cryptographic and packet processing tasks, and to verify the design on an FPGA platform. By offloading computation-intensive operations to hardware accelerators, the system achieves both flexibility (via ARM software for key management and protocol handling) and high performance (via hardware-accelerated encryption, authentication, and packet processing).


Project Objectives:

  1. Design a complete IPSec VPN module supporting ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) in tunnel or transport mode.
  2. Design dedicated IP acceleration cores for cryptographic operations (e.g., AES-128/256 for encryption/decryption, SHA-256/HMAC for authentication).
  3. Design optional acceleration cores for packet processing (e.g., IP header processing, sequence number verification, anti-replay check).
  4. Integrate the ARM processor and IP cores into an FPGA-based SoC system with Ethernet interface support.
  5. Verify the functionality, throughput, latency, and resource utilization of the system on an FPGA development board.


Expected Outcomes:

  1. A functionally verified IPSec VPN module on FPGA supporting ESP with encryption and authentication.
  2. Source code for ARM embedded software and IP cores (Verilog/VHDL).
  3. System block diagram, simulation waveforms, and on-board testing results (throughput, latency, resource utilization).
  4. Final project report and presentation.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

The rapid growth of large-model training, high-performance computing, and distributed storage has placed unprecedented stress on data center networks. Traditional protocols such as TCP/IP and static traffic scheduling policies struggle to satisfy microsecond-level latency requirements and hundred-gigabit throughput demands. AI training in particular generates synchronized burst traffic patterns that can rapidly overflow switch buffers, leading to packet loss and timeout-triggered retransmissions that are catastrophic for latency-sensitive distributed workloads. While loss-less networking technologies such as RoCE with PFC alleviate some of these issues, they introduce new problems including head-of-line blocking, congestion spreading, and even deadlocks. Consequently, intelligent path selection, end-to-end congestion control, and active queue management at switches have become central research topics in both academia and industry.



2. Main Task

This project requires the student to design and implement a complete network transmission control framework within a high-fidelity discrete-event simulation environment. The student must take full control of three categories of strategies. First, on the sender side, the student will implement multi-flow scheduling, congestion window management, packet segmentation, retransmission queues, and timer-driven timeout handling. Second, on the receiver side, the student will design reordering buffers, selective acknowledgement (SACK) generation, delayed ACK strategies, and buffer-overflow-aware feedback to the sender. Third, at the switch nodes, the student will implement multi-path routing decisions (e.g., ECMP, congestion-aware routing, packet spraying), priority-based queue scheduling, and AQM-style proactive dropping policies. All control logic must operate in a fully distributed manner, exchanging information solely through in-band packet fields, since no centralized controller or shared memory is available. The implementation must respect physical constraints such as link bandwidth limits, propagation delay, finite switch buffer capacity, and receiver memory limits.



3. Expected Outcomes

Upon completion, the student is expected to deliver:

(1) a fully functional Python implementation conforming to the interface, capable of guaranteeing in-order, lossless delivery of all flows across multiple benchmark datasets;

(2) a comparative evaluation of at least three congestion control variants and two multi-path routing strategies, measured in terms of flow completion time, throughput, deadline-miss rate, and final composite score defined by the contest scoring rule (weighted flow score multiplied by squared completion ratio);

(3) a thesis document including a literature review, system architecture diagrams, algorithmic pseudocode, experimental results with visualizations, and a critical discussion of trade-offs between fairness, latency, and throughput; and

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1) Organic mixed ionic-electronic conductors (OMIECs) are central to organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) and bioelectronics, where their swelling during ionic doping/dedoping critically influences device performance and stability. Existing techniques such as EQCM-D, AFM, and GIWAXS suffer from limited temporal/spatial resolution, inability for in-situ dynamic monitoring, or operational complexity. Recently, a high-resolution, real-time swelling-monitoring tool was developed in our lab, based on a customized laser Doppler vibrometer with mapping capability (LDV‑M).

The LDV‑M platform has enabled real‑time, high‑resolution mapping of swelling in OMIEC channels in conventional electrolytes (e.g., PBS). However, emerging electrolytes such as ionic liquids, hydrogel electrolytes, and bio‑inspired fluids exhibit unknown swelling behaviors due to their varied ion sizes, viscosities, and degrees of hydration. Understanding how these electrolytes dynamically affect OMIEC swelling is critical for developing next‑generation bioelectronics, neuromorphic devices, and implantable sensors. Yet, systematic monitoring of swelling across different electrolyte compositions remains unexplored.

2) This project will employ the established LDV‑M system to perform operando swelling monitoring of OMIEC channels in a series of emerging electrolytes, including ionic liquids, concentrated polymer electrolytes, etc. The study will map spatiotemporal swelling responses under varying gate frequencies, voltages, and cycling conditions. Key tasks include quantifying the magnitude of electrolyte‑dependent swelling, identifying transient ionic injection pathways, and correlating swelling behavior with device electrical performance and stability.

3) We expect to obtain comprehensive swelling‑electrolyte databases, revealing how ion species, mobility, and solvation affect OMIEC swelling kinetics and heterogeneity. The results will identify electrolytes that minimize parasitic swelling while maintaining high ionic conductivity, enabling more stable OECT operation.
rows.themeTitle: Swell Monitoring of Organic Mixied Ionic-Electronic Conductor in Emerging Electrolytes

This task aims to automatically identify and classify human behavior actions from visual or sensor data, providing perceptual intelligence for downstream decision-making. However, two major challenges remain in practical deployment: First, single-modality data (e.g., RGB images alone or point clouds alone) cannot simultaneously capture both appearance details and spatial structural information of human actions, leading to significant performance degradation under viewpoint changes and lighting variations. Second, existing multi-modal fusion methods typically rely on heavyweight architectures and large-scale annotated datasets, making them difficult to deploy on edge devices or real-time systems.

This project aims to leverage heterogeneous modality data fusion to achieve efficient and robust human activity recognition. The main contents include: 1. Theoretical foundations of heterogeneous data alignment and feature extraction from 2D (optical images) and 3D (radar point clouds/depth maps) modalities; 2. Designing a cross-modal fusion network that effectively integrates appearance features from 2D images with geometric features from 3D data; 3. Applying lightweight techniques to the fusion network to meet real-time inference requirements.

The anticipated project deliverables include: 1. A heterogeneous modality fusion network architecture for HAR; 2. Computer simulation results on public benchmark datasets; 3. Undergraduate thesis.

You can choose one or more programming languages such as C, C++, Python or MATLAB to realize your algorithms.

In the field of digital pathology, the automated analysis of whole slide images (WSIs) is a core task for assisting clinicians in cancer diagnosis and prognosis. However, in practical applications, two major challenges persist: First, WSIs are characterized by gigapixel-level resolutions and high costs for pixel-level annotation, which limits the effectiveness of supervised learning methods. Second, existing methods often overlook the contextual information of tumors and instance correlations, leading to misclassification.

This project aims to leverage weakly-supervised multiple instance learning (MIL) techniques to achieve efficient and accurate classification of histopathological images. The main contents include: 1. Mastering the fundamentals of medical image processing, weakly-supervised learning, and classic multiple instance learning theory; 2. Designing deep neural networks for WSI classification; 3. Investigating and implementing global context aggregation techniques into the network to capture the long-range dependencies among instances, overcoming the limitations of independent instance assumptions in traditional MIL.

The anticipated project deliverables include: 1. Design of a MIL-based WSI classification network; 2. Computer simulation and evaluation results on public datasets; 3. Undergraduate thesis.

To realize the algorithms, Python is highly recommended due to its mature ecosystem for pathology libraries. C++, C, or MATLAB may also be used based on specific requirements.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Background

Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM) communication is often considered to have inherent "physical layer security" due to its unique spatial structure. Unlike conventional plane waves, OAM beams require the receiver to be coaxially aligned with the transmitter to correctly decode the spiral phase information. If a receiver is off-axis or tilted, the orthogonality of the OAM modes is destroyed, leading to severe inter-mode crosstalk and a sharp rise in the Bit Error Rate (BER). This characteristic suggests that a "bypass eavesdropper" (Eve) located away from the main transmission axis might struggle to intercept the data, even if she is physically close to the legitimate path. However, as the OAM beam diverges during propagation, its

energy footprint expands, potentially leaking information to off-axis regions. For an undergraduate project, it is highly meaningful to simulate this security-performance tradeoff: analyzing how the misalignment (lateral offset and angular tilt) serves as a natural barrier against eavesdropping and determining the "secure zone" of an OAM link.


Main task

The student will first study the mathematical representation of OAM beams generated by Uniform Circular Arrays (UCA) and the strict requirements for coaxial alignment. On this basis, the student will implement a simulation platform consisting of one transmitter (Alice), one legitimate receiver (Bob) who is perfectly aligned, and one eavesdropper (Eve) who is located off-axis.

The simulation must model the "misalignment effect," where Eve’s receiving array is subject to lateral displacement (off-axis) and/or angular orientation errors relative to Alice. The student will calculate the received signal strength and the mode purity for both Bob and Eve. A key focus will be demonstrating that while Bob maintains high-quality communication, Eve’s reception efficiency drops significantly as her offset increases. The simulation should incorporate Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN) and consider the beam's natural divergence. After establishing the baseline, the student will analyze the "Secrecy Gap" or the difference in BER/SNR between the legitimate and eavesdropping links under various geometric configurations. While advanced information-theoretic proofs are not required, the model size should remain modest to stay within the expected undergraduate workload.


Expected outcomes

The expected outcomes include a complete final-year project thesis, a working MATLAB or Python simulation program, and a set of reproducible figures. The thesis should clearly explain the OAM transmission model, the coordinate transformation used to simulate misalignment, and the resulting impact on mode (orthogonality). The simulation results should include 2D/3D plots of energy leakage, mode purity vs. offset distance, and BER curves comparing the legitimate receiver and the eavesdropper. Representative comparisons should

include different OAM modes (higher modes diverge faster), varying propagation distances, and different levels of lateral/angular misalignment. The student should analyze the "security radius" of the OAM beam—the distance from the axis beyond which an eavesdropper cannot reliably recover the data. The project’s goal is to train the student in spatial electromagnetic modeling, security analysis in wireless communications, and technical document preparation.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

With the rapid growth of low-power Internet of Things (IoT) devices, wearable electronics, and consumer smart-home appliances, far-field wireless power transfer (WPT) is widely studied as a way to reduce the dependency on battery replacement. A practical WPT transmitter equipped with a MIMO array can apply transmit beamforming to direct the radio-frequency power towards the target IoT device. However, conventional MIMO beamforming concentrates the energy along the angle of the target device, while the energy still spreads along the entire range axis of that direction. This causes non-negligible spatial power leakage to other locations along the same angle, which is undesirable for both energy efficiency and electromagnetic-exposure considerations.

The frequency diverse array (FDA) introduces a small frequency increment between adjacent transmit elements, so that its transmit beampattern becomes a joint function of angle, range, and time. When combined with MIMO transmission, FDA-MIMO can synthesize a so-called dot-shaped range–angle beampattern, which focuses the transmitted energy not only on the angle of the target device but also on its range. This range–angle focusing directly addresses the spatial power-leakage limitation of conventional MIMO beamforming and is therefore attractive for civilian WPT to individual IoT devices.

For an undergraduate final-year project, it is meaningful to build a simple FDA-MIMO WPT simulation platform, design and compare several frequency-increment strategies, and quantitatively evaluate the received power, the energy harvesting efficiency, and the spatial power leakage. The project is purely simulation-based, focuses on civilian IoT and wearable scenarios, and does not involve hardware deployment.


2. Main task and division of labor

This is an individual undergraduate project. The student is responsible for literature review, simulation model construction, algorithm implementation, experiment design, result analysis, and thesis writing. The supervisor provides guidance on research scope, key references, milestones, algorithm feasibility, and report revision.

The student will first study the FDA-MIMO transmit beampattern, including the linear-frequency-increment configuration that produces the classical S-shaped range–angle beampattern, and at least one non-linear configuration such as logarithmically increasing frequency offsets that produces a dot-shaped range–angle beampattern. The student will then build an FDA-MIMO transmitter model, place a target IoT device at a configurable range and angle, and evaluate the radio-frequency power density across the range–angle plane.

On top of this platform, the student will (i) reproduce the conventional MIMO and the linear-frequency FDA-MIMO baselines, (ii) implement at least one non-linear frequency-increment design that produces a dot-shaped range–angle beampattern, (iii) compute the received power and the energy harvesting efficiency at the target IoT device, and (iv) compute the spatial power leakage ratio over a sample of non-target locations. The student will then study how these metrics vary with the number of transmit elements, the magnitude of the frequency

increment, the target range, and the design choice of the frequency-increment profile.


3. Expected outcomes

The expected outcomes include a complete final-year project thesis , a working MATLAB or Python simulation program, and a set of reproducible figures and tables. The thesis should clearly explain the FDA-MIMO transmit signal model, the linear and non-linear frequency-increment designs, the simplified energy harvesting model, and the evaluation procedure.

The simulation results should include three-dimensional power-density surfaces over the range–angle plane for the conventional MIMO baseline, the linear-frequency FDA-MIMO design, and the dot-shaped FDA-MIMO design. They should also include curves of received power versus target range, energy harvesting efficiency versus number of transmit elements, and spatial power leakage ratio versus the frequency-increment profile. The student should summarize the observations, discuss limitations such as the time-varying nature of the FDA beampattern and the dependence on accurate location knowledge of the target device.

1. Background

Cardiovascular diseases, including heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and valvular heart disease, remain major threats to public health. In primary-care and community-based scenarios, these diseases are often difficult to detect at an early stage due to limited diagnostic resources, dependence on clinician experience, and the lack of convenient point-of-care screening tools. An AI-enabled stethoscope provides a promising solution by integrating digital auscultation, single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), phonocardiogram (PCG), and artificial intelligence algorithms. Compared with traditional auscultation or single-modality ECG analysis, ECG-PCG multimodal fusion can simultaneously capture the electrical and mechanical activities of the heart, which is helpful for improving the robustness and interpretability of cardiovascular abnormality detection. Recent large-scale studies such as the

TRICORDER trial have shown that AI-enabled stethoscopes can acquire short ECG and PCG recordings during routine clinical examinations and provide AI-based screening results for heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and valvular heart disease. However, the trial also indicates that high algorithm accuracy in laboratory settings does not necessarily lead to real-world clinical benefits. Practical deployment, model efficiency, workflow integration, usability, and

local inference capability are also important factors that determine whether an AI medical device can be widely used. Therefore, for portable AI stethoscope applications, the algorithm should not only achieve acceptable diagnostic

performance but also be lightweight, deployable, and suitable for edge or mobile devices. Based on the laboratory’s previous work on ECG-PCG multimodal wearable cardiac monitoring systems, this graduation project aims to design and implement a lightweight ECG-PCG multimodal fusion algorithm for AI stethoscope applications. The project will focus on signal preprocessing, feature extraction, lightweight model design, multimodal fusion, performance evaluation, and edge deployment verification. The final goal is to develop an algorithm prototype that can receive ECG and PCG signals, perform local or edge-side inference, and output auxiliary cardiovascular abnormality risk analysis results.


References

[3]Raj S, Chand G S S P, Ray K C. Arm-based arrhythmia beat monitoring system[J]. Microprocessors and Microsystems, 2015, 39(7): 504-511.

[4]Caesarendra W, Hishamuddin T A, Lai D T C, et al. An embedded system using convolutional neural network model for online and real-time ECG signal classification and prediction[J]. Diagnostics, 2022, 12(4): 795.

[5]Kim J, Kim E, Kyung Y, et al. A study on ECG monitoring embedded systems[C]//2022 13th International Conference on Information and Communication Technology Convergence (ICTC). IEEE, 2022: 1671-1673.

[6]Liu W, Guo Q, Gao X, et al. Lead separation and combination: A novel unsupervised 12-lead ECG feature learning framework for Internet of Medical Things[J]. IEEE Internet of Things Journal, 2022, 9(23): 23897-23914.


2. Main Tasks

(1)Lightweight ECG-PCG multimodal signal analysis and fusion algorithm design.

(2)Design and implementation of deployable AI algorithms for portable AI stethoscope applications.

(3)Edge deployment optimization and diagnostic analysis software prototype implementation.


3. Research methods

(1)Lightweight ECG-PCG multimodal signal analysis and fusion algorithm design: Complete ECG and PCG signal preprocessing, including filtering, segmentation, normalization, R-peak detection, heart rate and HRV feature extraction, PCG envelope extraction, S1/S2 heart sound localization, and signal quality evaluation. Design ECG-only, PCG-only, and ECG-PCG fusion baselines. The fusion strategy may include feature-level fusion, decision-level fusion, attention-based fusion, or signal-quality-based adaptive fusion. The algorithm should focus on at least one cardiovascular abnormality detection task, such as atrial fibrillation detection, heart sound abnormality detection, valvular disease risk screening, or heart failure risk analysis.

（2）Design and implementation of deployable AI algorithms for portable AI stethoscope applications: Select lightweight and deployable model structures, such as 1D-CNN, depthwise separable CNN, temporal convolutional network, lightweight CNN-attention model, compact Transformer, traditional machine learning classifier, or TinyML-compatible neural network. Complete software-level modeling, training, validation, and testing using Python, PyTorch, TensorFlow, or scikit-learn. Compare single-modality and multimodal models in terms of accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1-score, AUC, negative predictive value, parameter size, and computational complexity. The model design should avoid unnecessarily large networks and should consider real-time inference on edge or mobile platforms.

（3）Edge deployment optimization and diagnostic analysis software prototype implementation: Optimize the trained model by model pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation, ONNX conversion, TensorFlow Lite conversion, or other lightweight deployment methods. Complete deployment verification on a PC-based simulated edge environment, Raspberry Pi, Jetson Nano, Android device, or other embedded platform. Record model size, inference latency, memory usage, and single-sample analysis time. Develop a simple diagnostic analysis software prototype that supports ECG-PCG signal input, waveform visualization, model inference, abnormality risk display, and structured analysis report generation. Finally, provide a comprehensive evaluation report and complete the graduation

thesis.

Baseline Model Implementation: Implement standard segmentation models (e.g., U-Net) trained solely on lateral annotations as baselines.

Unilateral Annotation Utilization Method Development: Design methods to leverage lateral annotations for segmenting both menisci. This may include symmetry-based constraints, semi-supervised learning strategies, cross-class knowledge transfer, or image registration and label propagation techniques.

Model Training and Validation: Train the proposed model using only lateral annotations, with a small set of medial annotations reserved exclusively for test evaluation.

Evaluation: Compare the proposed method against baseline models using quantitative metrics (Dice, IoU, Hausdorff distance) on the medial test set, complemented by qualitative visual inspection.


3. Expected Outcomes

  • Quantitative evaluation demonstrating the proposed method's performance on medial meniscus segmentation, validated on a small test set of medial annotations.
  • A project report documenting the methodology, experimental results, and analysis of the proposed approach and its limitations.

1. Background

Sleep quality is closely related to cognitive performance, emotional state, physical recovery, and long-term health. Wearable sleep-monitoring systems provide a practical way to collect physiological signals in daily environments, while an eye-mask structure is suitable for arranging frontal EEG electrodes, auxiliary stimulation electrodes, power-management circuits, wireless communication, and user interaction modules. Low-intensity electrical stimulation is a typical non-invasive neuromodulation technique. For an embedded wearable system, the key engineering tasks include stimulation-parameter configuration, waveform generation, constant-current output, output-current feedback, electrode contact and impedance detection, abnormal shutdown, and operation logging. Combining sleep-state monitoring with safe auxiliary stimulation can form an integrated eye-mask prototype that supports signal acquisition, state recognition, stimulation control, safety protection, and upper-computer visualization.

1. Background

Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA) is essential for diagnosing vascular diseases but requires intravenous contrast agent injection, which carries risks of allergic reactions and contrast-induced nephropathy. Non-contrast CT, while safer and lower-cost, fails to clearly visualize vascular structures. Generating synthetic CTA images from non-contrast CT using generative models offers a promising solution to obtain vascular information without contrast agent administration. However, a critical challenge lies in preserving vessel structure integrity, including main vessels, small branches, and vascular connectivity, as generative models often struggle to maintain fine-grained vascular details. Furthermore, existing image quality metrics are insufficient for evaluating vessel structure preservation. This project aims to develop generation methods that enhance vessel structure integrity and design corresponding evaluation metrics to quantify vascular preservation quality in synthetic CTA images.


2. Main Tasks

Data Preparation: Collect paired non-contrast CT and CTA datasets, perform preprocessing including registration, cropping, and normalization.

Baseline Model Implementation: Implement existing generative models for medical image translation as baselines for comparison.

Vessel-Structure-Aware Generation Method Development: Design and implement generation methods that enhance vessel structure integrity, potentially incorporating vessel segmentation guidance, topology-preserving losses, or attention mechanisms focused on vascular regions.

Evaluation Metric Design: Develop quantitative metrics to assess vessel structure integrity in generated CTA images, such as vessel coverage, connectivity, diameter preservation, and structural similarity indices.

Validation and Comparison: Evaluate the proposed generation and evaluation methods against baselines, demonstrating improvements in vessel structure preservation and the effectiveness of the proposed metrics.


3. Expected Outcomes

  • A vessel-structure-aware generation method for non-contrast CT to CTA translation that outperforms baseline models in preserving vascular integrity.
  • A set of quantitative evaluation metrics specifically designed for assessing vessel structure integrity in synthetic CTA images.
  • Comparative experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed generation method and the discriminative power of the proposed metrics.
  • A project report documenting the methodology, experimental results, and analysis of the proposed approaches.

Background:

Low-Earth-Orbit (LEO) satellite constellations are becoming a critical infrastructure for global broadband Internet access. Unlike geostationary satellites, LEO satellites orbit at altitudes of 500–1,200 km, causing rapid topological changes in inter-satellite links and frequent handovers between ground stations and satellites. Traditional static routing algorithms, such as Shortest-Path-First (SPF), rely on pre-computed routing tables that cannot adapt to dynamic link quality or congestion hotspots in real time.

Recent research has proposed distributed online learning approaches to address this challenge. The key idea is to treat each satellite as an independent learning agent that continuously observes local network conditions (e.g., queue length, link delay, neighbor availability) and selects the best next-hop neighbor using an online learning algorithm. The contextual bandit framework is particularly suitable because it balances exploration (trying potentially better routes) and exploitation (using currently known best routes) based on observed context features, without requiring a pre-trained global model or centralized control. This project explores the implementation and performance evaluation of such an adaptive routing mechanism for civilian LEO communication networks, based on an open-source ns-3 simulation framework.

Main Task:

The main task of this project is to implement and evaluate a contextual bandit routing algorithm on the ns-3 packet-level simulator. The student will first conduct a literature survey on LEO satellite network dynamics and online learning-based routing methods. The student will then study the core concepts of contextual bandit learning, including context feature extraction from local network state, the LinUCB (Linear Upper Confidence Bound) decision mechanism, and safety-constrained candidate filtering to ensure routing stability.

Based on this foundation, the student will implement the routing algorithm in C++ within the ns-3 framework, including: (1) a context extraction module that collects local network state features (e.g., queue utilization, link delay, hop distance) from each satellite node; (2) a decision module that scores candidate next-hop neighbors using the LinUCB algorithm and selects the best one; (3) a safety filter that restricts candidate selection to a stable subset (e.g., neighbors along SPF-computed paths or those making forward progress toward the destination) to prevent routing loops or black holes. The implementation will be evaluated on a standard Iridium-66 satellite constellation scenario with realistic Poisson traffic patterns, comparing the adaptive router against a dynamic SPF baseline in terms of flow completion rate, end-to-end latency, and packet drop rate.

The student will also conduct parameter sensitivity experiments to understand how the exploration-exploitation trade-off (controlled by the LinUCB exploration parameter alpha) and the safety filtering mode (relaxed, moderate, strict) affect routing performance. An optional extension is to evaluate the router under non-uniform hotspot traffic patterns to assess its load-balancing capability.

Expected Outcomes:

The expected outcomes include a working ns-3 simulation environment, an implementation of the contextual bandit routing algorithm with documented source code, experimental results comparing the adaptive router against the SPF baseline under varying traffic loads and parameter settings, and a final technical report describing the system design, implementation details, parameter analysis, and performance conclusions. The project will demonstrate practical engineering experience in network simulation, online learning algorithm implementation, and scientific experimentation, within the scope of an undergraduate final-year project.
rows.themeTitle: Design and Performance Evaluation of Contextual Bandit Routing for LEO Satellite Network Simulation
